senses.sense_definition: A letter, especially one that is long, formal, or didactic.

examples.text: The ambassador sent a lengthy <w>epistle</w> to the prime minister explaining the diplomatic crisis.
She spent the entire evening composing a furious <w>epistle</w> to the editor of the paper.

senses.sense_definition: One of the letters written by an apostle in the New Testament to an early Christian church or individual.

examples.text: The priest read a passage from the <w>epistle</w> to the Corinthians during the Sunday service.
Much of Christian theology is founded upon the theological arguments in each <w>epistle</w> of Saint Paul.

senses.sense_definition: A literary composition written in the form of a letter, especially one composed in verse.

examples.text: Horace was celebrated for writing a philosophical <w>epistle</w> in verse to his close friends.
The poet published a satirical <w>epistle</w> that mocked the corrupt manners of high society.

senses.sense_definition: A letter of dedication addressed to a patron or reader published as the preface to a literary work.

examples.text: The author included an <w>epistle</w> dedicatory praising the duke for his generous financial support.
Before the main text begins, an ornate <w>epistle</w> addresses the reader directly.

traits.comment: Used chiefly in early modern literature

senses.sense_definition: An extract from a New Testament letter or other non-gospel book read during a church service.

examples.text: The lector stood beside the altar to read the designated <w>epistle</w> for the feast day.
Silence filled the cathedral as the deacon completed the reading of the <w>epistle</w>.

senses.sense_definition: To write a letter to someone.

examples.text: He chose to <w>epistle</w> his friend rather than speak with him in person.
The scholar would frequently <w>epistle</w> distant colleagues about emerging archaeological discoveries.

traits.comment: Rarely used as a verb in modern English

senses.sense_definition: To write or compose something in the form of a letter.

examples.text: The philosopher decided to <w>epistle</w> his arguments in a series of open public dispatches.
Instead of an essay, she would <w>epistle</w> her observations to her mentor.

traits.comment: Rarely used as a verb in modern English

senses.sense_definition: To write letters; to engage in letter writing.

examples.text: After abandoning the law, he turned his energy to moral <w>epistling</w> and verse.
She spent her retirement <w>epistling</w> across Europe to preserve old friendships.

traits.comment: Rarely used as a verb in modern English

senses.sense_definition: To provide a literary work with an introductory epistle or preface.

examples.text: The dramatist sought to <w>epistle</w> the play before sending it to the printer.
The volume was richly <w>epistled</w> with an eloquent defense of ancient tragic verse.

traits.comment: Rarely used as a verb in modern English
